summary: Willisville fire tower, 24 m (80 ft), on Willisville Mountain in the Unorganized North Sudbury District; built in the 1920s and listed as removed.

facts.status_note: A lookout index lists the tower as removed. No source describes what, if anything, remains at the site.
facts.agency: Ontario Department of Lands and Forests

events.note: Fire ranger John (Jack) Burke started the visitors' journal at the tower. Wikipedia says he ran it in the early years.
A photograph caption places forest ranger Ernie Rogers in the tower cupola in May 1971.

evidence.supports: Built by the Ontario Department of Lands and Forests in the 1920s; 80-foot tower on Willisville Mountain
evidence.quote: An 80-foot fire tower was built on Willisville Mountain in the 1920s by the Ontario Department of Lands and Forests.

evidence.supports: Willisville and the tower lie in the Unorganized North Sudbury District
evidence.quote: It encompasses and provides services to the communities of Whitefish Falls and Willisville in the Unorganized North Sudbury District

evidence.supports: Willisville community lies on the Charlton-Cranberry-Frood Lake system within the La Cloche Mountains
evidence.quote: Willisville is on the Charlton-Cranberry-Frood Lake system in the heart of the La Cloche Mountains

evidence.supports: Tower layer lists a point named Burke Mountain Fire Tower
Lookout index files the Willisville tower under Burke Mountain
Lookout index lists the Willisville tower as removed
Fire ranger John (Jack) Burke started a visitors' journal at the tower on 12 July 1927; the blog says that may be when the tower opened
evidence.quote: Jack (John) Burke, the Fire Ranger, at the Willisville Fire Tower started a journal on July 12, 1927, which may be when the tower opened.

evidence.supports: The journal is a visitors' record: visitors were signed in with the date and origin
evidence.quote: 'Visitors to the Tower' were signed in with the date and where they were from.

evidence.supports: Burke ran the tower in its early years
evidence.quote: The tower was run by John Burke in the early years.

evidence.supports: While scanning for fires from the cupola, Burke saw elephants that had escaped from a circus truck
evidence.quote: One day, while he was looking out to spot forest fires from the tower's cupola, he saw a herd of elephants at the bottom of the mountain trail.

evidence.supports: Elephants had escaped from a circus truck that broke down nearby
evidence.quote: until locals learned that a circus truck had broken down nearby and the elephants inside had escaped.

evidence.supports: Joe Louis and Bing Crosby visited the tower and signed its guestbook
evidence.quote: World heavyweight boxing champion Joe Louis and singer Bing Crosby are known to have visited the tower and signed its guestbook.

evidence.supports: Forest ranger Ernie Rogers in the Willisville tower cupola, May 1971
evidence.quote: Ernie Rogers, Forest Ranger, in the Willisville Fire Tower cupola, May 1971

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The tower layer and the lookout index call the site Burke Mountain; Wikipedia places the tower on Willisville Mountain. The story treats these as one tower on one site, which is an inference from the matching names and the Willisville location.

notes_for_editor: Only Wikipedia gives the build: a 1920s tower built by the Department of Lands and Forests. The lookout index gives the removal, but no source gives a build year or removal date. 1927 is the first dated entry (a journal the blog says may mark the opening), so no built event is recorded; the events schema needs a year and Wikipedia gives only the decade. The tower is called Burke Mountain in the tower layer and the lookout index, and Willisville Mountain in Wikipedia; the story assumes one site. The brief record's status unknown is now gone, from one index only. Facebook caption (source 5) was read as the page title text only, so the quote is the caption. Still needed: removal date, what remains at the site, and whether the mountain is public land open to visitors (Archives of Ontario or Forest History Ontario, the La Cloche history group).
